To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
loss of PTEN is frequent in colorectal cancers and is associated with clinicopathological features but not dietary factors.

PTEN expression loss is a common event in CRCs but is independent of PIK3A mutations, that PTEN expression negative proximal CRC are of more advanced Dukse's stage and poor differentiation whereas PTEN expression negative distal CRC are of earlier Dukes' stages, that PTEN negative cancers were associated with lower blood LDL cholesterol, that PIK3CA gene mutations were more frequent in females and were not associated with any specific dietary factor.
PTEN expression was frequently lost in colorectal cancers and that proximal cancers were more likely to be PTEN expression negative and of a more advanced Dokes' stage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the PTEN gene in colorectal cancer, a common disease in the western world.
the molecular mechanisms that drive tumour development and the role of diet and lifestyle in the aetiology of CRC.
understanding how diet may affect cancer risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PTEN loss is an independent prognostic marker for CRC.
PTEN is frequently inactivated in colorectal tumours and that dietary factors are unlikely to be associated with this inactivation.
PTEN loss of function in CRCs is associated with clinicopathological features and not with dietary factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PTEN loss of function may be a key event in the development of colorectal cancer, which is associated with poor prognostic indicators, but not with dietary factors.
PTEN expression is lost frequently in colorectal cancers but the mechanisms for this are unclear.
the PTEN gene is frequently inactivated in colorectal cancers by a mechanism that is independent of PIK3A mutations and is associated with clinicopathological features.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PTEN loss is common in CRC and that it is not associated with any specific dietary factors.
PTEN expression status is associated with tumour clinic-pathological features and that this association differs between proximal and distal cancers.
loss of PTEN is not related to dietary factors and that PTEN expression status is not a good prognostic indicator in colorectal cancer.
